title: Ranveer Singh Walked Out of Don 3 Weeks Before Filming. ₹45 Crore Later, Even Aamir Khan Couldn’t Fix It.
excerpt: FWICE issued a non-cooperation directive. Excel claims massive pre-production losses. Ranveer’s camp says the script was never finalized. The franchise war Bollywood has been whispering about is finally public.
body:
There is a version of this story where **Ranveer Singh** plays Don for the third time, strides onto a massive set in some undisclosed European location, and delivers one of 2026's biggest films. In that version, everyone makes money, the franchise lives on, and nobody calls the union.

That version does not exist.

What exists instead is a ₹45 crore dispute, a formal non-cooperation directive from the **Federation of Western India Cine Employees (FWICE)**, and the uncomfortable revelation that even **Aamir Khan** — a man who literally makes films about resolving impossible conflicts — could not broker a peace deal between Ranveer and the franchise's makers.

The facts, as laid out by **FWICE chief adviser Ashoke Pandit** in a Hindi Rush interview, are blunt. **Farhan Akhtar** and **Ritesh Sidhwani** of **Excel Entertainment** filed a formal complaint after Ranveer exited *Don 3* just weeks before cameras were scheduled to roll. The filmmakers claimed they had already burned through approximately ₹45 crore on pre-production — hotel bookings, location scouting, overseas travel arrangements for a crew of over 200 people. All of it, smoke.

> "Many people from the industry, including Aamir Khan, had been trying to resolve the issue before it came to us. That also didn't work." — Ashoke Pandit, FWICE

Ranveer was officially announced as the new Don in August 2023, stepping into a role that **Shah Rukh Khan** had owned for two stylish instalments. The casting was bold, the anticipation enormous. For a while, everything seemed to be moving.

Then ***Dhurandhar*** happened.

Ranveer's 2025 spy thriller — directed by **Sriram Raghavan** and produced by **Dinesh Vijan** — became a phenomenon, crossing ₹1,100 crore net in India. It did not just make Ranveer a bigger star. It fundamentally altered his leverage, his market position, and apparently his appetite for a project whose creative terms had shifted beneath him.

Sources close to Singh paint a picture of escalating frustration: the script allegedly never reached a finalized state, storyline arcs remained unresolved, and the film's reported budget was slashed from ₹300-350 crore to approximately ₹150 crore. Ranveer's camp also maintained he had never received an advance for the project. From their perspective, this was not a walkout — it was a project that was no longer the project he had committed to.

Excel saw it differently. They saw a star who committed, an entire production machine built around that commitment, and a sudden departure that left them holding a ₹45 crore bill with nothing to show for it.

The fallout was extraordinary by Bollywood standards. FWICE sent formal notices to Ranveer — multiple times, over a month and a half. No response came. When Singh's team finally replied, they argued the matter fell outside FWICE's jurisdiction entirely. "We wanted Ranveer to come, sit, and solve this issue," Pandit said. "But he said that this is not your jurisdiction, you don't have to do anything with this issue."

On May 25, FWICE issued a non-cooperation directive — not a ban, Pandit carefully clarified — instructing its four lakh members across 32 craft associations not to work with the actor. The directive was eventually withdrawn after Ranveer's representatives engaged with the federation. But by then, the damage to the optics was done.

Pandit's most revealing comment, though, was not about the directive. It was about what came before it.

"Aamir Khan discussed the issue before it came to the federation. That also didn't work. So, I think when a man is successful, it's important for that person to move around with people."

That is a politely devastating line.

For the Indian diaspora, this is not just industry gossip. The *Don* franchise is a cultural artefact — the original 1978 film starring **Amitabh Bachchan** is embedded in NRI memory, and SRK's 2006 reboot became a touchstone for a generation that grew up toggling between Bollywood and Hollywood. The question now looming over the franchise: does it survive this rupture, and if so, who wears the suit next?

For Ranveer, the calculus is cold and clear. After *Dhurandhar*, he is arguably the most commercially powerful actor in Hindi cinema. He can afford to walk away from a project. Whether the industry can afford to let its biggest star walk away from a ₹45 crore commitment without consequence — that is the question this dispute was really about.

The non-cooperation directive is gone. The ₹45 crore question is not.
